analysis.one_liner: Charges market prices for federal grazing, mining, timber, oil, gas, irrigation, and park concessions.
analysis.headline: With 59 cosponsors including 57 Democrats, the bill sat in three House committees without a hearing or vote and died when the 105th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have ended decades-old bargains in which the federal government sells public resources cheap: it required fair-market prices for grazing land, timber, mining claims, oil and gas leases, rights-of-way, and irrigation water, imposed a 5 percent royalty on gold and other hardrock mining, banned timber sales that cost taxpayers more than they bring in, and replaced the National Park concessions system with competitive bidding. The money would have reduced the deficit and paid to clean up abandoned mines and improve parks.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who currently fund the difference between bargain prices and fair market value on federal minerals, forage, timber, and water; park visitors, who would gain from competitive concession bidding with fees directed back into park maintenance; and people living near abandoned hardrock mines, whose cleanup would be funded by a new mining royalty.

how_it_helps.text: Bars any federal agency from selling timber, minerals, forage, water, or federally generated hydroelectric power for less than fair market value.

Imposes a 5 percent royalty on hardrock mining under the 1872 mining law and channels the money, plus claim maintenance fees, into an Abandoned Minerals Mine Reclamation Fund to clean up abandoned mine sites.
Sets grazing fees on national forest and public domain lands at fair market value using a formula, and dedicates receipts to fish and wildlife habitat, riparian restoration, and enforcement.

Phases out below-cost national forest timber sales between 1998 and 2002, requiring each sale's revenue to exceed the government's full costs, and requires land managers to identify economically unsuitable timberland.
Requires ranchers and farmers receiving subsidized federal irrigation water to pay full delivery cost and cuts their federal farm payment limits by the value of the water subsidy.

Replaces fixed $1-$10 per acre oil and gas lease rentals with fair market rentals, raises right-of-way permit prices to fair market value, and lets Interior assess a 20 percent penalty on underreported oil and gas royalties.

Repeals the 1965 National Park Concessions Act and requires concession contracts to be competitively awarded, with franchise fees deposited into a Treasury account or Park Improvement Fund for park upkeep, and ends preferential renewal rights for most large contracts.

analysis.who_pays: Hardrock mining companies, federal grazing permit holders, timber purchasers, oil and gas lessees, utility and pipeline right-of-way holders, and large farms receiving subsidized irrigation water — all of whom would begin paying closer to market rates for public resources. Existing contracts were grandfathered for five years, and a presidential waiver allowed exceptions.
analysis.who_pays_short: Mining, ranching, timber, and oil and gas interests

drawbacks.text: The bill repeals the Emergency Livestock Feed Assistance Act of 1988, eliminating a disaster program that helped ranchers facing feed shortages.

Higher grazing fees and an end to below-cost timber sales would raise costs for small and large operators alike, and reduced federal timber volume could mean job losses in timber-dependent rural communities, a cost honest supporters of market pricing generally acknowledged.

Some increased costs — for grazing, minerals, and timber — could be passed on to consumers through higher meat, wood, and mineral prices, since permit holders facing new fees are the ones setting market prices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have transferred money from subsidized commercial users of public land to taxpayers and public lands programs, with a clear environmental side benefit from abandoned-mine cleanup and riparian restoration. The honest costs are real but narrower: some rural communities built around cheap federal timber and grazing would have faced painful adjustments, and the repeal of feed assistance removed a disaster safety net. On balance it is a straightforwardly pro-taxpayer bill whose burdens fall mainly on commercial permit holders, including some small ranchers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Resources, Agriculture, and Budget Committees and dispatched to seven subcommittees, but no committee ever acted on it, and it died when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Rep. George Miller of California introduced the bill on March 4, 1997, with 35 original cosponsors.
The bill gathered 59 cosponsors in total — 57 Democrats, 1 Republican, and 1 Independent.
It was referred to three full committees (Resources, Agriculture, and Budget) and to seven subcommittees, with executive comment requested from the Agriculture and Interior Departments.
The last recorded action was a subcommittee referral on March 18, 1997; no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever occurred before the Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hardrock mining companies, grazing permit holders, timber purchasers, and oil and gas lessees kept their below-market access to federal resources; incumbent park concessioners kept the 1965 rules and their preferential renewal rights.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Mining, grazing, timber, and oil companies

for.name: Rep. George Miller
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 35 original cosponsors on day one.

for.name: 59 cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support, 57 Democrats, 1 Republican, and 1 Independent.

against.name: Don Young
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill out of committee; it was sent to four Resources subcommittees and never scheduled for a markup.

against.name: Robert Smith
against.what_they_did: Never acted on the bill, which contained the grazing fee, irrigation subsidy, and livestock feed assistance provisions in his committee's jurisdiction.

sides.party_line_note: Support was nearly all Democratic — 57 of 59 cosponsors — and the Republican chairs of the committees that received the bill took no action on it in two Congress years.

industries.note: A 5 percent royalty, $100-$125 annual claim fees, and a cutoff on new mining patents would end the 1872 mining law's practice of letting companies extract gold and other metals from public land without paying royalties. The royalty would have funded cleanup of abandoned mines, a cost taxpayers currently absorb.

Grazing fees on national forest and BLM land would rise to fair market value under a set formula, ending the below-cost fee formula set by executive order. Grazing advisory boards dominated by permit holders would be abolished.

Below-cost national forest timber sales — sales where the government loses money on road building, sale preparation, and administration — would be phased out by 2002, cutting off timber supplied at taxpayer expense.

industries.industry: Oil and gas lessees on federal land
industries.note: Fixed rentals as low as $0.50-$10 per acre would be replaced with fair market rentals, and a 20 percent assessment would apply to significantly underreported royalties.

industries.industry: Large farms receiving subsidized federal irrigation water
industries.note: Farms growing program crops on federally irrigated land would pay full water delivery cost and have their federal payment limits cut by the subsidy value of the water — a direct reduction in stacked agricultural subsidies.

Competitive bidding, a 10-year contract cap, and franchise fees flowing to the parks would end the 1965 system's protections for incumbents, but existing concessioners would keep possessory interests in their improvements and smaller operators (under $500,000 in receipts) and outfitting guides would keep preferential renewal rights.
